actors.label: Log on disk and page cache

frames.narration: A teaching walk-through with round numbers, not a measurement. A producer has a batch of small records for a topic. The record's key picks partition 2, so the batch goes to the broker that leads that partition.

messages.label: batch of records, key picks partition 2

frames.narration: The leader appends the batch to the end of the partition's log. The file is only ever added to at the end, which is the linear disk I/O the 2014 post stresses. Each record gets the next offset: here, 40 to 43.

The follower acts like a consumer of the leader's log. It fetches the new records and writes them to its own copy. This is how the post describes replication: the replicas are really nothing more than a specialized consumer.

Now the acknowledgement. In the post's asynchronous test, the leader could have answered as soon as its own write was done. In the synchronous test it waits until all in-sync replicas have the batch, as shown here, and then tells the producer the batch has offsets 40 to 43.

A consumer asks for records from the offset it last saved. The post says consumers are only given messages that all in-sync replicas have acknowledged, so a record it sees will still exist if the leader fails and another copy takes over.

The leader sends a chunk of the log straight from the file to the network (the post names the sendfile call), usually out of the operating system's page cache because the data was just written. The consumer processes the records and later commits the next offset, 44, so that a replacement could resume from there.
